traits: Pencil-width mud tubes climbing a foundation, pier, or garage wall
Swarmers have a straight waist, straight antennae, and four equal-length wings
Daytime swarms, typically on warm afternoons in late winter and spring
Discarded wings (four, all equal length) scattered on windowsills or the attic floor after a swarm

look_alikes.difference: Termite swarmers have a straight waist and straight antennae; carpenter ant swarmers have a pinched waist and elbowed antennae.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from the side on the waist and antennae of a winged individual.

copy.what_it_means: Mud tubes or swarmers suggest subterranean termite activity, but they don't prove it on their own — other insects and debris can look similar. An inspection is what confirms active termites and how far they've spread.
copy.fact: The mud tubes are climate-controlled highways — termites dry out fast, so they build covered roads between soil and wood.
copy.blurb: What's in the photo is consistent with subterranean termite activity — mud tubes, swarmers, or wings. A photo can't confirm termites; an in-person inspection can.

tech_notes: Photo ID is SUGGESTIVE ONLY — never report as a WDO finding. Verify tubes/frass/wings on-site; distinguish ant vs. termite swarmer (waist, wing pairs, antennae).

traits: Big dusk swarms around lights, concentrated in a few weeks each spring
Swarmers yellowish-brown, slightly larger than native subterranean swarmers
Soldiers exude a white glue-like defensive substance when disturbed
Carton nest material (looks like packed cardboard) sometimes visible in walls or trees

look_alikes.difference: Formosan swarmers are slightly larger, more uniformly yellowish-brown, and swarm in far bigger numbers over a shorter spring window.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of several swarmers next to a coin, plus the time of evening and date.

copy.what_it_means: Swarms like this near lights in late spring are consistent with Formosan termites, among the most destructive termites in Florida — but a photo doesn't confirm the species or how far a colony has spread. An inspection does, and scopes any treatment.
copy.fact: A mature Formosan colony can hold millions of termites — they’re called "super termites" for colony size, not for how they bite.
copy.blurb: A mature Formosan colony can hold millions — they’re called "super termites" for colony size, not bite.

tech_notes: Photo ID is SUGGESTIVE ONLY. Confirm via soldier defensive secretion + swarmer size vs. native Reticulitermes. Check for carton nests in trees/walls.

traits: Tiny six-sided pellets in neat piles under a pinhole-sized opening in wood
No mud tubes — the colony lives entirely inside dry wood, no soil contact
Swarms at dusk, often after a warm rain, mainly in spring
Blistered or peeling paint over wood that sounds hollow when tapped

look_alikes.difference: Drywood termite pellets are hard, six-sided, and uniform; carpenter ant frass is fibrous sawdust mixed with insect parts.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the pellet or debris pile on a light-colored surface.

copy.what_it_means: Pellet piles under a pinhole in wood are the classic drywood termite "kick-out" sign. Pellets are evidence of drywood termite activity — they don't confirm whether the colony is still active or how far it's spread through that wood. An inspection determines that and scopes any treatment.
copy.fact: Those pellet piles are "kick-out" debris — the colony sweeps its gallery and pushes the pellets out a hole the size of a pin.
copy.blurb: The photo shows signs consistent with drywood termites — often the tell is small piles of pellet-like frass. Only an inspection can confirm whether the colony is active.

tech_notes: Photo ID is SUGGESTIVE ONLY. Six-sided pellets vs. carpenter-ant frass (fibrous). Map kick-out holes; check fascia, window frames, furniture.

traits: Soldiers have a teardrop-shaped head with a round pore (fontanelle) on the forehead that can release a milky defensive fluid
Pale, creamy-white workers that avoid light
Swarmers are caramel-colored with wings and fly mainly February through May, often at dusk
Colonies can hollow out large living trees as well as structural wood

look_alikes.difference: Both are Coptotermes with a teardrop soldier head and a milky-oozing fontanelle pore; told apart only by soldier head-hair pattern under magnification
look_alikes.next_photo: A technician confirms the species from a soldier sample collected on-site — a photo alone can't separate these two Coptotermes species

copy.what_it_means: An invasive termite that has been spreading in parts of Florida and can build large colonies quickly, in trees as well as homes. A photo suggests this species but can't confirm it or the extent of any damage — that takes an in-person inspection and, for a firm species call, a lab-checked sample.
copy.fact: It is a tropical relative of the Formosan termite and can hollow out large, healthy trees as well as structural wood.

tech_notes: Confirm via soldier head hair pattern under magnification; visually similar to C. formosanus, cannot be split by eye alone. Full inspection for colony extent, moisture/wood contact, and tree infestations before any treatment.

review.notes: Species-level soldier ID is a magnification-level distinction from Formosan termite; app photo ID should stay suggestive only and route to inspection, per brief hard rule. Per audit item 53: traits[0] reworded from 'oozes ... when squeezed' to avoid inviting a customer to squeeze/handle a termite soldier.

traits: The largest termite found in Florida, with swarmer wings over half an inch long
Found in damp or decaying wood, especially dead branches on living trees, stumps and old fence posts
Does not build mud tubes and does not need soil contact
Swarms mainly in late fall and early winter, unlike most other Florida termites

look_alikes.difference: Dampwood termite is much larger and lives only in damp or decaying wood; drywood termite is smaller and infests dry, sound wood with no moisture problem
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo with a coin next to the wings or the insect for a size comparison

copy.what_it_means: A large termite that lives in damp, decaying wood — most often dead limbs on live trees, old stumps or wet fence posts. It's rarely a threat to sound structural wood on its own, but a sighting near the house is worth an inspection to check for a moisture problem.
copy.fact: It is the largest termite in the eastern United States, with swarmers whose wings can be longer than half an inch.

tech_notes: Uncommon structural pest in SE US; usually indicates chronic moisture/decay rather than a colony threat to sound wood. Inspect for the moisture source; confirm species vs drywood/subterranean before any treatment recommendation.

review.notes: Verdict judgment call: IFAS describes this species as not economically important in the southeastern US, so set to watch rather than call; owner may prefer call to stay consistent with other termite entries. Per audit item 37: safety.structural changed from true to false to match this entry's own copy ('rarely a threat to sound structural wood on its own') and rule 6 (structural only when the organism damages sound structural material; this species needs already-damp/decaying wood, not sound wood).

traits: Two pairs of wings that are equal in length and both extend well past the body
Straight, bead-like (not elbowed) antennae
Thick waist with no pinch between thorax and abdomen
Often found near light fixtures or window sills with a scatter of shed wings and few or no bodies left behind

look_alikes.difference: Termite swarmers have equal-length wing pairs, straight antennae and a thick waist; ant swarmers have unequal wings, bent antennae and a pinched waist
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from directly above showing the waist shape and whether the wing pairs are equal length

copy.what_it_means: Winged termites leaving a mature colony to start new ones nearby — one of the clearer warning signs of termite activity in or near a home. A photo can flag the shape, but only an inspection can find the colony and confirm the species.
copy.fact: A swarm can release thousands of winged termites at once, but only a tiny fraction survive to start a new colony.

tech_notes: Photo ID is suggestive only; confirm species (subterranean vs drywood vs Formosan/Asian) and locate colony with full inspection before treatment recommendation.

review.notes: Peak months checked against three UF/IFAS EDIS species pages: native subterranean termites swarm Reticulitermes hageni (early Dec-early Feb), R. flavipes (Jan-Apr) and R. virginicus (Feb-late May) per IN369; Formosan subterranean termite swarms April-June, peak May, per IN278; drywood termite (Cryptotermes cavifrons) swarms year-round with peak March-May per IN537. Combined, this supports a Jan-June peak window rather than a single exact figure -- this entry deliberately stays a blended, multi-species estimate (as its own copy and tech_notes already say), not a claim that one set of months is exact for every species swarming in SWFL. Returned to draft after removing generic alate aliases, which can mean winged ants or termites; owner re-approval is required. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Thin, pencil-width tunnels of packed dirt running up a foundation, pier or wall
Usually found where wood meets soil or concrete, often hidden behind siding, mulch or stored items
Surface crumbles easily and reveals a hollow tunnel and sometimes live termites inside
Tubes can be dry and abandoned or currently active with soft, moist mud

look_alikes.difference: Mud tubes are built tunnels of packed dirt on a surface; drywood termite frass is loose piles of tiny pellets with no tunnel structure
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up showing whether the material is a solid tube or a loose pile of pellets

copy.what_it_means: Subterranean termites build these tubes to travel safely between the soil and the wood they're feeding on. A tube is evidence of activity, but it doesn't say whether it's still in use — finding one, dry or moist, is a strong reason for an inspection rather than guessing from a photo.
copy.fact: The tubes exist because subterranean termites need to stay moist; the mud shields them from open, dry air as they travel.

tech_notes: Break open a short section to check for live termites/moisture before deciding active vs relic. Full inspection for extent and entry points; do not treat off a photo alone.

traits: Tiny, oval pellets, about the size of ground pepper, uniform in shape
Pellets are pushed out of small round 'kick-out' holes in wood and pile up below or on nearby surfaces
Color ranges from light tan to dark brown depending on the wood
No mud, webbing or tunnel structure attached to the pile, unlike mud tubes

look_alikes.difference: Termite pellets are uniform, ridged ovals with rounded ends; roach droppings vary in size and shape and are often mixed with egg cases
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the pile showing whether the pieces are all the same uniform shape.

look_alikes.difference: Frass is a loose pile of dry pellets with no structure; mud tubes are solid, built tunnels of packed dirt
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up showing whether the material is a loose pile or a solid tube

copy.what_it_means: Drywood termites, and less often dampwood termites, push pellets like these out of the wood they feed on, so a pile points to termite activity in that wood. It doesn't show which kind, whether the colony is still active, or how far it's spread; an inspection determines that.
copy.fact: Drywood termites push these pellets straight out of their tunnels to keep their living space clean, which is often the only visible sign of an infestation inside sound-looking wood.

tech_notes: Look for the kick-out hole near the pellet pile; sound the surrounding wood. Full inspection before any treatment recommendation.

traits: Small, papery, translucent wings scattered on a windowsill, floor or in a spiderweb, with few or no bodies
Usually appears suddenly after a warm evening, often following rain
Wings are shed in pairs, so look for whether the two pairs on each side are the same length or not
Found near light fixtures, windows or doors where the swarm was drawn to light

look_alikes.difference: If the shed wing pairs on each side are the same length, the swarm was termites; if the front pair is clearly longer than the back pair, it was ants
look_alikes.next_photo: A close, well-lit photo of a few wings laid flat, showing the length of both pairs

copy.what_it_means: A pile of shed wings with no bodies means a swarm happened nearby, and wing shape is the fastest way to suggest whether it was termites or ants. Either way, a swarm indoors means a colony is close by, so it's worth an inspection to find it and confirm what it was.
copy.fact: Swarmers shed their wings within minutes of landing because a pair that has already mated has no more use for flight.

tech_notes: Wing-pair length ratio is the key photo clue for termite vs ant; confirm with full inspection to locate the parent colony regardless of which it turns out to be.

review.notes: This entry's own design already avoids the overclaim in the verification note: it never asserts a wing pile is always termites (sign_of lists both termite-swarmers and winged-ants, copy says wing shape is what 'suggests' termite vs ant, and tech_notes call for a full inspection either way). Ants also shed their wings after a mating flight (see the winged-ants entry's own traits), so a bodies-free wing pile can genuinely come from either group; role/risk default to the more consequential possibility (termites) as a cautious default pending the wing-length check, which matches how this entry is actually written.
